subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Anirban, and I was standing two rows behind Abhinav at the rally. On Friday he had said, “Everyone from tuition is going, so I'm going,” and when I asked what the march wanted, he shrugged and laughed. Today he waved a paper flag at strangers. Then the crowd near the barricade began shoving, and somebody shouted that the road was closing. Abhinav's laugh stopped. “Which way is the gate?” he asked me. I didn't know either; neither of us had checked. He grabbed his friend's sleeve and we pushed sideways for ten minutes, his water bottle gone and his phone nearly dead. I can't say what he felt, but he kept muttering, “What are we even here for?” Finally a shopkeeper let us sit inside, and Abhinav rang his mother from the shop.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav go to the rally?
qa.a: Everyone from tuition was going, so he went too.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling when he asked which way the gate was?
qa.a: Fear and confusion: his laugh stopped and he kept asking what they were there for, which suggests he did not know what he was supporting or how to leave.

qa.q: What could Abhinav have done before going, and why would it help?
qa.a: He could have found out what the march demanded and agreed a leaving route and a check-in with a parent, because then he would know what he was backing and how to get out.

qa.q: How does the day look to Anirban, who tagged along?
qa.a: Anirban was pulled into the same confusion with no exit plan either, and could only guess at Abhinav's feelings while trying to find a safe way out.

grounding: A teen joins a protest because friends do, without knowing the demands, and is lost when tension rises.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: risk assessment and safety planning [Action]
passage: When our school's eco club announced a rally to save the old park trees, I wanted to go, but Mummy's face said no before her mouth did. So I made a checklist. First I read the notice again: the district office had given permission and the organisers called it a peaceful gathering. Then I told my parents the exact spot, the gate near the library, and that it would run from four to six. My uncle Zubin agreed to come along. I packed two bottles of water and charged my phone to full, and Uncle and I decided that if the crowd got tight or the mood changed, we would leave by the library lane at half past five at the latest. Mummy still looked worried, but she stopped saying no. Standing there with my sign, I felt calm, because the exit was already decided. — Imran

qa.q: Where did Imran tell the family the rally would be?
qa.a: At the gate near the library, from four to six.

qa.q: How did Imran feel at the rally, and what explains it?
qa.a: Calm, because the exit was already decided and the plan had been checked with the family.

qa.q: What could Imran do if the parents still refused, and why?
qa.a: Imran could back the cause another way, such as signing a petition or helping with a school poster, because it keeps the aim without adding risk the family is not comfortable with.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the plan?
qa.a: Mummy still looked worried, but a known place, set timings, an adult companion and a fixed leaving time gave her something concrete to trust.

grounding: A teen checks the protest is permitted and peaceful, tells parents the place, goes with an adult, packs supplies and agrees a leaving time.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: talking with parents and weighing their concerns [Action]
passage: “Honestly, nobody believes me when I say I didn't argue.” I'm Sabina, and last month a students' march was planned over leaked exam papers. My father, Wasim, said no at once: board prep, crowds, all of it. Instead of shouting, I asked him to tell me every single thing he was scared of. He listed three: getting hurt, losing revision time, being filmed. Then I told him why it mattered, that my cousin lost a whole year because of the leak. Ammi sat down and listened as well. In the end we made a deal. I wouldn't go to the march itself. I'd make posters with the school group at home on Saturday and join the small signature table outside our colony gate. Abbu even carried the posters out. Part of me still wanted to be there, but it felt fair.

qa.q: What three things was Wasim scared of?
qa.a: Getting hurt, losing revision time and being filmed.

qa.q: What might Sabina have been feeling about the deal at the end?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: part of Sabina still wanted to be at the march, but the outcome felt fair because both sides had been heard.

qa.q: What could Sabina try if the parents had refused any kind of taking part, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could write a letter or speak at a school forum from home, since it voices the concern while keeping the family's trust.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Wasim?
qa.a: His worries about safety and revision were listened to and answered, so he could accept a smaller way of taking part and even help carry the posters.

grounding: A teen listens to parents' worries, explains why the issue matters and agrees a limited form of participation.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: choosing other lawful ways to contribute [Thinking]
passage: “Come sit, Gudiya, and I'll tell you about the bus-route marches of my school days. I'm Rekha, your Dadi. I was fifteen, and half the town was marching for a new school bus. Asif from my class kept saying, ‘Only cowards stay home.’ That stung. But I sat on the veranda and counted on my fingers. March: I'm small, Papa won't allow it, and crowds get wild. Petition: forty signatures by Friday, easy. Letter to the councillor: one evening. Speaking at assembly: frightening, but the principal listens. Then I asked myself what I truly wanted. A bus. Not my face in a crowd photograph. So I did the petition and the assembly speech. Asif still grumbled that I had hidden. But in March the route was changed.”

qa.q: How many signatures did Rekha think she could collect by Friday?
qa.a: About forty, which she called easy.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when Asif said only cowards stay home?
qa.a: It stung, so she felt hurt and pressured, but she still sat down to think it through.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rekha's choice, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking herself what she truly wanted, a bus and not a photograph in the crowd, showed that a petition and an assembly speech could reach that aim within her age and her father's limits.

qa.q: How might Asif have seen Rekha's choice?
qa.a: Asif grumbled that she had hidden, so Asif probably saw staying out of the march as playing safe, and may not have noticed that the petition and speech were lawful ways to get the same result.

grounding: A teen weighs a petition, a letter, an assembly speech and marching, and picks lawful options that fit age and risk.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: sharing unverified posts as action [Pitfall]
passage: Dear Ramesh Sir, you asked why the class group was full of arguments on Monday. Partly, that was my fault. On Saturday night a forwarded message said students had been beaten at the candle march and hospitals were overflowing. It came with a photo, and I felt my chest burn. Within a minute I had sent it to four groups, thinking I was helping the cause. By Sunday afternoon a classmate whose brother was really at the march told us the message was old and from another city. Two friends had already posted furious comments. Now half the class thinks the organisers lied, and one girl refuses to sign our petition. I should have checked before pressing send. I am sorry. Yours, Vidya

qa.q: How many groups did Vidya forward the message to?
qa.a: Four groups, within a minute.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the message arrived?
qa.a: Anger and alarm: Vidya's chest burned and the urge to act at once made forwarding feel like helping.

qa.q: What could Vidya have done instead of forwarding straight away, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could have checked the photo and its date with a reliable source or asked a teacher first, because a quick check would have stopped a false claim spreading and protected the cause.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Sir see the class arguments?
qa.a: Ramesh Sir sees a class divided by a false message and wants to understand how it started, so Vidya's honest account helps Ramesh Sir deal with it.

grounding: A teen forwards dramatic unchecked messages as action, and the false message causes confusion and weakens the cause.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: avoiding any decision out of fear [Pitfall]
passage: The evening news showed crowds outside the collectorate, and Neelam switched it off. “I'm not thinking about any of this,” she told her brother Raghav, who was reading about the student council election. “Politics means trouble.” At school, the civics teacher asked for volunteers to debate the flooded drain outside the gate, and Neelam kept her eyes on her desk. When her friends planned an email to the ward councillor, she said she had a headache and left early. Weeks later the drain still overflowed every rainy morning. A friend said, “You write so well, Neelam. You could have helped us.” She had no answer. She didn't know how a petition worked, or what a lawful march looked like, because she had made sure never to learn.

qa.q: What did Neelam do when the news showed crowds?
qa.a: She switched it off.

qa.q: What was Neelam afraid of when she avoided the debate and the email?
qa.a: Getting into trouble; she said politics means trouble, and staying away felt like the way to avoid the risk.

qa.q: What could Neelam try instead, and why?
qa.a: She could take one small lawful step, such as helping a teacher draft the email to the councillor, since it teaches how public life works while keeping the risk low.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Neelam's decision?
qa.a: Raghav, who cares about the student council election, may see her as capable but closing a door before learning what safe taking part looks like.

grounding: A teen avoids all civic thinking out of fear, staying safe but losing the chance to learn lawful participation.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: changing plan when the situation shifts [Revision]
passage: Arohi and I had planned to go to the river-cleaning rally on Sunday; she had even printed a banner. I'm Sabina, her classmate, and I was at her flat at breakfast when she went quiet over the local news. “Gathering has turned tense,” she read out. “Officials say the crowd is far bigger than expected.” She put her phone down. “I don't think we should go.” I reminded her that we'd made a plan. “The plan was for a peaceful morning,” she said. She texted her aunt to cancel the lift, then messaged the eco club: “Can I help with the awareness table in the colony park instead?” By noon she was folding leaflets, humming. I'd guess she was a bit disappointed, but she never said so.

qa.q: What did Arohi read on the news at breakfast?
qa.a: That the gathering had turned tense and the crowd was bigger than expected.

qa.q: What does Arohi's humming while folding leaflets suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: That she felt settled about the new decision, though Sabina guesses Arohi may also have been a little disappointed.

qa.q: What else could Arohi do to judge the risk, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a trusted adult to read the latest updates with her, because a second view helps her judge whether it is safe; the awareness table already let her help without the tense crowd.

qa.q: How might Arohi's aunt see the cancelled lift?
qa.a: The aunt probably sees a careful teen changing plans sensibly and is relieved that Arohi is staying away from the tension.

grounding: A teen drops a planned protest when news says it is tense and joins a peaceful awareness activity instead.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
passage: Sunday night. The signature march for the library fund is over and I'm too wired to sleep, so I'm writing. What I learned: the organisers kept to the route, and a volunteer with a whistle kept the lines neat. I hadn't known that most of it is waiting. What felt bad: when a stranger began shouting at people on the pavement, my stomach dropped and I moved next to Jahnavi ma'am. Did it work? Honestly, maybe forty people watched. But the councillor's assistant took our letter, and that's something. I'm not sure I'm the shouting type. Tomorrow I'll ask Jahnavi ma'am how to join the school committee so I can help plan things like this properly. Small steps. — Ira

qa.q: Who took the group's letter?
qa.a: The councillor's assistant.

qa.q: What did Ira feel when the stranger began shouting?
qa.a: Uneasy: Ira's stomach dropped and Ira moved closer to Jahnavi ma'am.

qa.q: How else could Ira stay involved, and why might it work?
qa.a: Ira could write to the councillor or help make posters, since these suit Ira's comfort with noise; the committee also lets Ira help plan events carefully.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi ma'am see Ira asking about the committee?
qa.a: Jahnavi ma'am, who stood beside Ira during the uncomfortable moment, would likely see a student who thought through the day and wants to take part responsibly.

grounding: After a peaceful gathering a teen reviews what was learned, what was uncomfortable and how effective it was, and chooses the school committee.

passage: Dear Nazia, you asked why I've been so quiet. Papa wants me to skip the robotics camp in June and run our stationery shop during the wedding-season rush. At first I only felt a knot in my stomach, so I took a page and drew a line down the middle. Under Family Duty I wrote: Papa not working alone, being the child he can count on, the shop that paid for my school bag. Under My Ambition I wrote: building the sensor arm, proving a girl from our lane can do it, a certificate for engineering colleges. Looking at both, I saw they were about the same thing: being trusted and becoming someone. The knot got smaller. I still don't know what I'll tell him, but now I know what I'm choosing between. Write back? Arohi

qa.q: What did Arohi write under My Ambition?
qa.a: Building the sensor arm, proving a girl from our lane can do it, and a certificate for engineering colleges.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling before writing the two columns?
qa.a: A knot in the stomach: confused and torn, unable to separate the feelings until they were on paper.

qa.q: What could Arohi try next, and why?
qa.a: Ask Papa what the shop truly needs in June and suggest half-days, because facts might replace the either-or and let both needs be met.

qa.q: How might Papa see the request to skip the camp?
qa.a: Papa probably sees a busy shop and needs a dependable helper, and may not yet know what the camp means to Arohi.

grounding: A girl writes down what family duty and her own ambition each mean so the conflict is understood, not only felt.

passage: In the school counselling room, Joseph tapped his pencil on a sheet of paper. “My parents want me at the shop all June, and the robotics camp is in the same month,” he said. “So it's yes or no.” Trisha, the counsellor, only asked, “Is it?” Joseph frowned and began to write. “Mornings at the shop and afternoons free. My sister could take the afternoon shifts, she's free after her exams. Or the shorter programme in the city, that's two weeks, not four.” He crossed out the words yes or no. “That is three options, not two,” he said, half laughing. Trisha said he could take the list home instead of an answer. He folded it into his bag, feeling lighter than when he had come in.

qa.q: How long is the shorter programme?
qa.a: Two weeks, not four.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after crossing out yes or no?
qa.a: Relieved and a little amused: he half laughed and left feeling lighter.

qa.q: What could Joseph do with the list, and why?
qa.a: He could show it to his parents and ask which option suits the shop best, because talking it through lets them choose together.

qa.q: How might Joseph's sister see the plan?
qa.a: She may be surprised at being asked to cover afternoon shifts, but a limited task after her exams is easier to accept, and she would want to be asked first.

grounding: A student widens the choice beyond yes or no by listing half-days, a sibling covering shifts and a shorter programme.
